title: Built-in Value Types
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behavior of built-in value types in C#.
Choose an appropriate type for a simple application scenario.
Read and explain original C# code that demonstrates the lesson concepts.
Predict deterministic program output and identify common mistakes.
Compile and execute a small .NET 10 console example to verify the result.

understand.concept: C# value types store their data directly as a value. The built-in simple value types include integral numbers, floating-point numbers, decimal numbers, bool and char. Assigning a value type copies its value, so changing one variable does not change another variable that received a copy.
understand.whyItMatters: Choosing the correct value type helps represent data accurately, avoid accidental truncation and make program intent clear.
understand.analogy: A value-type assignment is like copying the number written on a card: each card can be changed independently.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy describes assignment behavior, not the physical memory layout. Struct values can contain references, and runtime storage details depend on context.

explain.narrative:
## What is a value type?

A value-type variable contains a value of its declared type. The built-in simple types include signed and unsigned integer types, float, double, decimal, bool and char. C# also supports user-defined structs and enums.

## Copying values

Assigning one value-type variable to another copies the current value. Later assignments to one variable do not update the other. This differs from assigning a class or array reference.

## Choosing a type

Use integral types for whole numbers, decimal for base-10 financial calculations, float or double for approximate floating-point calculations, bool for true/false state and char for one UTF-16 code unit.

## Baseline

Examples target .NET 10 and C# 14. Numeric ranges and conversions are explored in the next lessons.

examples.title: Copy an integer value
examples.explanation: The assignment copies the current int value. Updating copy does not change original.

examples.title: Use decimal for a price
examples.explanation: The m suffix creates a decimal literal. Decimal is useful when base-10 precision is important.

examples.title: Store a Boolean state
examples.explanation: bool represents one of two logical values and is a value type.

examples.title: Store a character
examples.explanation: A char stores one UTF-16 code unit. Casting this basic Latin character to int displays its numeric code unit value.

examples.title: Copy a floating-point value
examples.explanation: The two double variables hold independent copied numeric values. double uses binary floating-point representation.

questions.prompt: Which built-in C# type represents true or false?
questions.explanation: bool stores one of the two Boolean values: true or false.

questions.prompt: What happens when an int value is assigned to another int variable?
options: Both variables become one shared reference
questions.explanation: Value-type assignment copies the current value.

questions.prompt: Which literal suffix identifies a decimal literal?
questions.explanation: The m or M suffix identifies a decimal literal.
C# char is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit, not a complete arbitrary-length text string.

questions.prompt: Which type is intended for true/false state?
questions.explanation: bool communicates a logical state directly.
